title: Chevron Stock (CVX) Holds Flat as Gulf Bypass Plans Target 60% of Hormuz Oil - TechStock²
content: Chevron Corporation NYSE:CVX finished Wednesday almost unchanged, even as oil held near recent highs. Brent settled at $88.98 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate ended at $83.27. The muted stock move points to a longer investor debate. Gulf states are spending heavily on routes that bypass Hormuz. Those projects could erode part of today’s oil risk premium. The long-term buildout is substantial. Projects under discussion could add 3.8 million barrels daily by end-2027. Added capacity may reach 7.3 million by end-2028. That equals 31.7% of the Gulf’s 23 million-barrel prewar export base. That future capacity does little for today’s bottleneck. Kpler tracked eight Hormuz vessels on Tuesday. The prewar range was 125 to 140 daily. Traffic is therefore about 94% below the range midpoint. Simon-Peter Massabni of XS.com said markets increasingly doubted a quick agreement could ease crude disruptions. Demand is the counterweight. OPEC cut 2026 demand-growth expectations to 580,000 barrels daily. The IEA expects demand to contract by 1.6 million bpd. Chevron has already converted the disruption into earnings and cash. Second-quarter adjusted profit reached $12.0 billion. Worldwide output rose 20% to 4.07 million oil-equivalent barrels daily. Chevron’s advantage is geographic. Its Middle East production is smaller than several peers. That allows the company to capture higher benchmark prices with less regional output loss. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria called its latest quarter “robust operational performance and strategic consistency.” Reuters Wall Street remains constructive but not unanimous. The average 12-month target was $215. Forecasts ranged from $170 to $236. One strong-sell rating remains against 19 positive recommendations. Risks cut both ways. Renewed attacks could lift crude and Chevron’s upstream profit. A ceasefire, weaker demand or faster pipeline completion could remove the premium. Refining margins can also reverse quickly. The practical investor test is timing. Bypass projects matter most after 2027. Current shipping data still governs near-term prices. Chevron’s $18.1 billion quarterly free cash flow provides the bridge between those two horizons. That combination usually matters more than the daily gain itself. CVX is still in an uptrend, with the SMA20 at 190.59 rising at 1.69% over 5 days and the share price holding above both the SMA20 and the SMA50 at 183.37. In plain language, the short-term average is above the longer-term average, and price is above both, which tells traders the recent move has not been a one-day spike but part of a broader climb. There is no fresh MA-cross, so the market is not flashing a new regime change; instead, it is extending an existing one. The stock is also sitting near the upper edge of its recent range, with a 3-month high of 198.87 and a 3-month low of 164.78. That matters because price near the top of the range often means the market has already repriced a good portion of the near-term optimism. As shown in the chart, the latest close is only a step below the visible ceiling. One more detail sharpens the picture: the 20-hour resistance at 196.83 is effectively being tested, while the 20-hour support at 181.60 remains well below. Price is at 99% of the range, which signals strength, but also leaves less room for complacency. The momentum tools are telling a more nuanced story. The RSI at 61.2 is still in a neutral zone, which means the stock is not yet in a classic overheated condition on that measure. But the Stochastic %K at 91.3 versus %D at 57.9 is overbought, showing that CVX has moved quickly enough to stretch short-term momentum. In practical terms, stochastic often reacts faster than RSI, so this reading suggests the rally may be mature even if it has not fully exhausted itself. The MACD at 2.960, just above the signal line at 2.958, with a tiny positive histogram of 0.002, still points to positive momentum. That spread is narrow, though, which means the bullish impulse is present but not especially forceful. Strong trends usually show a cleaner gap between MACD and signal; here, the market is advancing, but it is doing so without much acceleration. Volatility appears contained rather than explosive. Volume adds another caution flag. The latest volume was 6,046,100, below the 20-day average of 7,818,450, or 0.8× normal. That tells us the move higher is not being backed by unusually heavy trading. In technical analysis, rising price on lighter volume can still work, but it is less convincing than a rally powered by broad participation. The OBV is rising, though, which means cumulative volume flow still favors the bulls even if the latest session was not especially busy. The market is now focused on a narrow band of decision points. The first line to watch is the 196.83 resistance, which sits just above the last price. A clean move through that zone would put the stock into open air toward the 198.66 Bollinger upper band and then the 3-month high at 198.87. If price cannot clear that area, the stock may simply remain capped near the top of its range. On the downside, the nearest structural floor is the 190.59 SMA20, which doubles as the Bollinger middle band and is therefore an important pivot. Below that, the more meaningful support is 182.51 at the lower Bollinger band, with the broader 181.60 support just beneath it. A drop through that zone would weaken the case that the current trend is still intact. In a video posted Sunday on Truth Social, U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. military would continue bombing Iran until its objectives are achieved, warning operations remain ongoing and acknowledging additional American casualties are likely. Trump confirmed that U.S. and Israeli forces had struck hundreds of targets across Iran, including Revolutionary Guard facilities and air defences, while calling on Iranian military and police to surrender “for full immunity or face certain death.” The U.S. military also confirmed its first combat losses in the conflict, with three servicemembers killed and five seriously wounded in an Iranian counterattack. Erin Koegel, co-chair of the House Commerce Finance and Policy Committee, aims to prohibit the virtual currency kiosks across the state. The state currently has about 350 licensed kiosks operated by eight to 10 companies, according to the Department of Commerce. The bill was introduced on Monday and discussed on Thursday to prevent the rising scams against the elderly of the state. Police told lawmakers on Thursday that scammers tell victims to put cash into these machines. The money is turned into cryptocurrency and sent to accounts controlled by the scammers. Once sent, it is very hard to track or get back. They added that the scams were mostly hurting senior citizens. Woodbury Detective Lynn Lawrence told the House that officers once found an older woman confused at a gas station crypto kiosk. She had already made “at least 10 Bitcoin transactions in six months.” Lawrence added that the woman “had been giving 50% of her income per month to the scammers” and was scared she might have to live in her car. The Department of Commerce reported 70 complaints last year totaling $540,000 in losses. Refunds averaged only 16% of total losses. title: Chevron (CVX) Signed A 20 Year AI Data Center Power Deal - Sahm
content: Chevron (CVX) Signed A 20 Year AI Data Center Power Deal This kind of long term pairing between energy producers and AI infrastructure providers is becoming a theme worth tracking. It is especially relevant if you want to compare Chevron's approach with other companies in the same space through 56 AI infrastructure stocks Chemron sits in a part of the market where energy demand tied to data and computing has become a key talking point for investors. The stock trades at US$186.56, with returns of 19.7% year to date and 26.7% over the past year. The value_score of 3 suggests some investors may still view it through a more traditional energy lens rather than a data infrastructure supplier. Project Kilby gives Chevron a 20 year view on supplying power to Microsoft AI data centers using its natural gas platform, with carbon capture and renewable power planned over time. This is different to traditional upstream and refining projects because it ties Chevron directly into data center energy demand rather than only commodity markets. For you as an investor, it adds a long dated infrastructure style revenue stream alongside a business that already reported US$70.1b in Q2 2026 revenue and US$12.1b in net income. The existing Narrative for Chevron focuses on low cost production, tight oil supply and refining margins as key supports for future cash returns. Project Kilby introduces a new angle. It links those hydrocarbon assets to AI power needs and to Chevron’s early work in carbon capture and lower carbon fuels. The risk side does not go away. Chevron is still heavily exposed to hydrocarbons, project execution and regulation, so the question is whether long term AI power deals materially offset those pressures or simply sit alongside them. The clearest early signal is whether Chevron can sign one or two additional long term AI data center power contracts in other U.S. gas regions using the same template. If similar deals appear over the next 12 to 24 months, it suggests Project Kilby is becoming a repeatable business line rather than a one off agreement. The mix of natural gas, carbon capture and renewables in those follow on projects will also show how far Chevron can align this model with tightening policy and compliance expectations. The bank has a ‘Buy’ rating on the oil and gas company and a $210 price target on the shares, implying around 19% upside from Wednesday’s close. CVX stock was down nearly 1% at the time of writing on Thursday. “CVX is our preferred way to play [increased oil prices] … integrateds are pricing in <$70/bbl LT Brent, which we see as a particularly attractive entry point,” Bank Of America (BofA) said in a note to clients, according to a report in CNBC. “We prefer CVX to XOM given its Venezuela presence, lack of Middle East exposure, and higher earnings torque to the shifts upward in prices in 2026/27,” the firm added. The Iran war has pushed crude prices higher amid concerns over supply disruptions, with control of the Strait of Hormuz at the center of the conflict. The waterway handles around 20% of global oil shipments, making any disruption a major risk for energy markets. However, oil futures dipped slightly on Thursday. At the time of writing, International Brent crude futures (Co1) were down 2.56% at $76 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate futures (CL1) fell 2.3% to $71.83 a barrel. Despite Thursday’s slight dip, Bank of America expects oil prices to remain elevated as the U.S. continues its campaign against Iran and brushes off efforts to reach a settlement. “Medium term restocking demand should support a $70/bbl level, assuming that the strait reopening is not essentially flawless from here, which seems like a safe assumption (at least as of today),” the BofA analyst wrote. Yet, ExxonMobil's stock has outperformed Chevron's over the past five years. Big oil companies have traditionally been considered reliable dividend payers, but with the wave of extra cash that they've seen coming in this year, you can bet they'll get more shareholder-friendly. Chevron(NYSE: CVX) and ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM), the two largest American oil companies, have long been the standard for big oil dividend payers. The difference is what they primarily focus on. Chevron operates more in the upstream segment, drilling and extracting oil. ExxonMobil has a much larger downstream presence, refining crude oil into refined products such as gasoline and plastics. ExxonMobil's business is larger and more diversified than Chevron's, but Chevron is known for its leaner, more efficient operations. If you're focused on maximizing your passive income right now, Chevron is the better choice. At the time of writing, Chevron's dividend yield is 3.7% compared to ExxonMobil's 2.7%. Both are admirable and not stopping anytime soon, but ExxonMobil's is longer nonetheless. Although Chevron offers a higher yield, ExxonMobil would be a good go-to if you prefer a stock with stronger overall growth opportunities. title: XOM, CVX Stocks In Focus: Trump Criticizes Exxon And Chevron For Profiting From Iran-Driven Oil Price Surge — ‘They’re Making Too Much Money’ - Stocktwits
content: President Donald Trump criticized Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) and Chevron Corp. (CVX) on Monday, saying the oil giants made “too much money” as crude prices surged during the Iran war. He urged them to lower gasoline prices for consumers. Shares of Chevron were down 2.3% in afternoon trading, while Exxon Mobil was trading 0.8% lower. Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said, “They’re making too much money based on a shortage. I don't like it,” according to CNBC. According to TheFly, Trump added, “I should be the last one to say because I’m a big free enterprise guy, nobody bigger. You surprised I’m saying it? I’ll say it loud and clear. I’m not happy about it.” Trump also said, “Chevron, too much money. ExxonMobil, too much money. They’re going to give some of that back to the public and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price,” CNBC reported. The remarks come as higher gasoline prices, driven by the Iran war, and broader cost-of-living concerns pose a political risk ahead of November’s midterm elections, when Republicans are seeking to retain control of Congress. Trump also criticized Chevron Chief Executive Mike Wirth for not highlighting his administration’s pro-fossil fuel policies during an interview with Fox Business Network. Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, “The only thing he conveniently forgot to mention ⁠is that, without the genius, foresight, strength, and stability, of the TRUMP Administration, the Oil Industry, and our Country itself, would be DEAD!" On the Fox Business interview, Wirth said Chevron was producing record amounts of oil in the U.S. and refining record volumes of crude. Trump also told oil companies to “get your consumer (retail!) Oil Prices DOWN, NOW!” Trump’s criticism comes days after Exxon Mobil and Chevron reported blockbuster second-quarter earnings as the Iran war pushed energy prices higher. Exxon Mobil’s quarterly profit more than doubled from a year earlier to $14.5 billion, its highest level since 2022, while Chevron posted record quarterly earnings of $12.1 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal. Omeros Corporation said on Monday that U.S. Medicare officials have approved extra payments to hospitals that use its newly launched drug YARTEMLEA to treat a rare and often deadly complication of stem cell transplants. Shares of the company were trading 4% higher at the time of writing. Starting October 1, hospitals can receive up to about $287,000 more from Medicare for each qualifying patient under the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ new status for the therapy. The extra funds go straight to the hospitals to help cover the high cost of the new treatment. Omeros itself will still receive the same payment for the drug. YARTEMLEA is the only medicine approved in the United States for this transplant complication, known as TA-TMA. The condition damages small blood vessels and can be life-threatening, especially for the kidneys. About three in 10 patients who receive the more complex type of stem-cell transplant in the U.S. are covered by Medicare. Company CEO Gregory Demopulos said the decision should make it easier for hospitals to choose the drug based on what patients need, rather than worrying about the cost. YARTEMLEA reached the market earlier this year after winning FDA approval in late 2025. It is Omeros’ first commercial product and the main source of near-term revenue. The company is counting on growing sales of the drug to help fund the rest of its research pipeline, which includes longer-lasting versions of similar medicines, experimental cancer therapies, a potential treatment for cocaine addiction, and other programs aimed at hard-to-treat conditions. BlackRock (BLK) on Monday launched two tokenized money market funds, deepening its push into blockchain-based cash products for stablecoin issuers and crypto-native investors. The BlackRock Select Treasury Based Liquidity Fund (BSTBL) now has a tokenized share class issued on Ethereum (ETH), with BNY Mellon (BNY) as transfer agent and tokenization provider, the company stated. A second vehicle, the BlackRock Daily Reinvestment Stablecoin Reserve Vehicle (BRSRV), was launched,  with Securitize (SECZ) as transfer agent and tokenization provider, and intends to qualify as eligible reserve assets for permitted US payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act. "As demand grows for high-quality reserve assets to support stablecoins and other tokenized financial products, these funds provide clients with additional choice in how they access and use money market fund investment solutions across traditional and digital markets,” said Jon Steel, Global Head of Product and Platform for BlackRock's Cash Management business. BlackRock first disclosed the products during its second-quarter earnings call last month, when Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Martin Small had said the filings were "about bringing BlackRock's core cash management capabilities to where digital assets clients are already operating." Small added that as stablecoins and digital wallets grow, "clients will need high-quality reserve and liquidity products that can operate natively in that digital ecosystem." The launch came after BlackRock’s BUIDL fund, its first tokenized money market offering, launched with Securitize in March 2024 and has since grown to around $2.5 billion in assets. BUIDL’s price continued trading at $1 during the past 24 hours. The retail sentiment around BUIDL remained in the ‘neutral’ zone, while chatter around it stayed at ‘high’ levels over the past day. CVX Testing Key Resistance…Waktu & Kalender Chevron Corp. shares rose to 194.91 on the NYSE, up 4.48% from the previous close of 186.56, according to Yahoo Finance data cited at 10 August 2026 20:30 WIB. The move pushed the stock back into the upper end of its recent trading band, with price now sitting near the top of the 20-day range and just below the latest resistance zone. In plain terms, the market is paying up for CVX again, but the chart is now close to an area where sellers have recently shown up.Energy & Utilities The broader structure remains constructive. Chevron is still in an uptrend, helped by the SMA20 at 189.84 rising at a 1.74% pace over the past five days, while the SMA50 at 183.09 sits below it. That positioning matters because it shows the shorter-term average is already above the longer-term one, a classic sign that momentum has improved even without a fresh moving-average crossover. The absence of a new MA-cross means the rally is being extended rather than freshly triggered, which often makes the next test of resistance more important than the last breakout.Energy & Utilities The price is also trading above the middle Bollinger band at 189.84, with the upper band at 198.28 and the lower band at 181.40. That places CVX in the upper half of its volatility envelope, but not yet at an extreme. The stock is already at 87% of its 20-day range and has moved within striking distance of the 196.83 resistance level. That combination usually signals a market that is still trending, but one where follow-through needs to be proven rather than assumed. The oscillator picture is more mixed than the price trend. The RSI at 59.5 is neutral, which means the stock is neither stretched nor washed out. That is important: it leaves room for further gains, but it does not confirm a momentum surge. The Stochastic %K at 76.5 versus %D at 36.8 points to short-term strength, but the gap between the two lines also suggests the move may be getting ahead of itself. In practical terms, Stochastic above 70 often means price is nearer the top of its recent range, not that a reversal is guaranteed. The most cautionary signal comes from MACD at 2.647, which remains below its signal line at 2.973, leaving a -0.326 histogram. That negative histogram means upside momentum is still lagging the trend in price. So while the chart says Chevron is advancing, the oscillator setup says the advance has not yet fully re-accelerated. This is the kind of divergence traders watch when a stock climbs into resistance: price is strong, but the internal thrust is only moderate. Volatility is contained rather than explosive. The ATR at 4.98, equal to 2.6% of price, indicates a normal trading environment, not a disorderly one. The Bollinger band width of 8.9% is also described as normal, which suggests the stock is not in a squeeze that would foreshadow a sharp breakout, nor in an expansion phase that would imply unusually large swings. In other words, CVX has room to move, but the chart does not yet show the kind of compression that typically precedes a major directional release. Volume, however, is doing more of the talking. The latest session recorded 13,652,700 shares, about 1.7x the 20-session average of 7,856,580, and OBV is rising. That matters because rising volume alongside a price advance suggests participation is broad enough to support the move. If the rally had come on thin trading, it would have looked more fragile. Instead, the surge in turnover says institutions and larger market participants likely had a hand in the day’s strength. The nearest support sits at 181.60, just above the lower Bollinger band at 181.40. That confluence is meaningful: if price loses that area, the chart would be signaling that the recent rebound has failed to hold its own volatility floor. On the upside, 196.83 is the immediate resistance to watch, while the broader three-month high stands at 198.87. Those two levels form a tight overhead zone, and the market is now close enough that the next move could decide whether CVX pauses, breaks through, or rolls back into the middle of its range. If Chevron clears 196.83 decisively, the chart would be pointing toward a retest of the 198.87 three-month high. If it fails there, a retreat toward 189.84 would fit a normal pullback to the Bollinger midline and the SMA20. If that fails, the 181.60 support becomes the key line separating a healthy consolidation from a deeper unwind. - Reason 2: Volume and OBV are confirming participation, so the move is not isolated.
- Reason 3: MACD remains below its signal line, showing momentum is still not fully aligned with the price advance. - Verdict invalidated if price breaks below 181.60, because that would damage the current support structure and put the lower Bollinger band in play. - Ideal Entry Range: 189.84 to 181.60 on a pullback that holds the SMA20 and support zone.
- Exit Target: 196.83, with 198.87 as the next chart reference if resistance gives way.
- Stop Loss protection: below 181.40 to 181.60, using the lower Bollinger band and nearby support as the risk boundary. For non-traders: the chart is still healthy, but CVX is close enough to resistance that it makes more sense to wait for confirmation than to assume the next move will be upward. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is set to rule on five closely watched treatments in August from Moderna, Lantheus Holdings, Bristol Myers Squibb, Capricor Therapeutics and Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical. Decisions are due by August 23 at the latest on therapies ranging from an mRNA flu vaccine to a gene therapy for a rare metabolic disorder, putting biotech investors on high alert as the outcomes could drive sharp near-term moves across the sector. Moderna is seeking approval for mRNA-1010, its experimental mRNA-based seasonal flu vaccine for adults 50 and older. An FDA advisory panel already voted unanimously in favor of the shot in June, and the FDA is slated to decide on its application by August 5. The FDA initially refused to file Moderna’s application in early February 2026, citing concerns that the comparator vaccine used in the main trial did not reflect the best available care for older adults. Moderna revised its plan, and now the company is seeking a traditional approval for adults aged 50-64 and an accelerated approval for adults 65 and older. If granted accelerated approval in the patient population, Moderna will be required to conduct another study to confirm effectiveness in the group. Lantheus wants approval for MK-6240, a PET imaging agent that detects tau protein tangles in the brain, a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease. Doctors would use the scan to help confirm the presence of tau pathology, stage the disease, and guide treatment decisions. The FDA accepted the company’s application seeking approval in October and granted it a fast-track designation. The application is based on two late-stage trials in people with early Alzheimer’s disease. In both trials, the scan identified patients with tau pathology and ruled out people without it, to support the application. The FDA will decide on the application by August 13 at the latest. Bristol Myers Squibb is seeking approval for iberdomide, an oral drug combined with existing medicines for patients whose multiple myeloma has returned or stopped responding, by August 17. It works by helping the immune system attack cancer cells more effectively while also directly killing myeloma cells. Bristol Myers’ application was accepted by the FDA in February and granted priority review. The application relies on the large late-stage trial where iberdomide, together with Daratumumab and Dexamethasone, showed a statistically significant improvement in minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity rates compared to control arms. MRD negativity means no detectable cancer cells remain after treatment — an early sign of deep response. Capricor is seeking full approval for Deramiocel, a cell therapy aimed at heart damage caused by Duchenne muscular dystrophy. After an earlier rejection, the company submitted new data from its late-stage HOPE-3 trial to the FDA. However, in July, an advisory committee voted 9–3 against the claim that the available evidence provides substantial proof of effectiveness for treating DMD cardiomyopathy. The vote is non-binding, meaning the FDA could still approve the therapy. Ultragenyx is seeking approval for DTX401, a one-time gene therapy for glycogen storage disease type Ia, a rare inherited metabolic disorder, by August 23. People with GSDIa cannot release stored sugar from the liver, leading to dangerous drops in blood sugar (hypoglycemia) during fasting, excess glycogen buildup in the liver and kidneys, and other long-term complications. The FDA granted priority review to Ultragenyx’s application in February. There are currently no approved treatments that address the underlying cause of GSDIa. Energy majors have spent recent stretches navigating a market defined by swinging crude prices, uneven refining margins, and a structural pivot toward electrification that has forced long-established producers to rethink how they allocate capital. Against that backdrop, a name with the scale and diversification of the company in focus tends to draw scrutiny not because it is flashy, but because it is steady. The energy sector as a whole has been treated by many market participants as a place to find durable cash generation rather than rapid expansion, and that framing has only strengthened as broader equity benchmarks have climbed to levels that leave many growth-oriented names looking stretched on a pricing basis. The quarterly update that landed recently gave this narrative another data point. Rather than showing strain from a choppy commodity backdrop, the company posted figures that pointed toward resilience, a description that market watchers have increasingly applied to integrated energy operators capable of absorbing swings in crude pricing through the balance of upstream production, midstream logistics, and downstream refining. That resilience is precisely the quality that tends to appeal to those weighing energy names through a value lens rather than a momentum one. Understanding why this update carried the weight it did requires stepping back to look at how the business actually operates. The company runs an integrated model spanning upstream exploration and production, a global network of refining and chemical assets, and a marketing arm that touches fuel retail in numerous regions. This structure is deliberate. When crude pricing softens, the downstream refining and chemicals side can act as a partial offset, since lower input costs can support margin even as upstream revenue per barrel declines. When crude pricing firms, the upstream side captures the benefit directly. That built-in balance is part of why integrated majors are often treated differently from pure-play exploration names when market participants assess resilience through cycles. Operationally, the company has also leaned into large-scale, long-life projects that are designed to generate steady output over extended periods rather than short bursts tied to a single commodity cycle. This includes deepwater developments, liquefied natural gas infrastructure, and a growing footprint in some of the lowest-cost production basins globally. The logic behind this positioning is straightforward: assets with lower breakeven costs tend to remain economically viable across a wider range of crude pricing environments, which in turn supports steadier cash generation and, by extension, steadier capital distribution to equity owners. The recent quarterly disclosure did more than simply beat the prior comparable period on a top-line basis. It also showed an operating margin that improved relative to the same stretch a year earlier, an outcome that tends to carry particular weight in the energy sector because margin performance there is often treated as a proxy for how well a company is managing costs, throughput, and mix even when commodity pricing itself is not moving dramatically in one direction. Sentiment around the name firmed measurably in the aftermath, with market commentary framing the update as evidence that capital discipline exercised over recent periods was translating into tangible earnings strength. That kind of reporting season narrative tends to matter more for value-oriented energy names than for growth names, precisely because the market participants who gravitate toward this corner of the sector are typically weighing steady execution against a backdrop of modest pricing multiples. A quarter that reinforces the case for durable cash generation, rather than one that surprises with a dramatic swing in either direction, tends to be read as confirmation of an existing narrative rather than a reason to substantially reprice the stock. That appears to be roughly how the market treated this particular update, with firmer sentiment following the release rather than a dramatic repricing event. One of the more closely watched elements of any energy major's quarterly disclosure is what happens with cash returned to equity owners. In this case, the company maintained its cash distribution, extending a long streak of consistent payouts that has become a defining feature of its reputation among market participants who track energy value names specifically for their capital discipline. Maintaining a distribution through a period of commodity volatility signals confidence in underlying cash generation, and it also reflects a broader capital allocation stance that has prioritized steady payouts and disciplined spending over aggressive expansion. This approach stands in contrast to earlier eras of the energy sector, when producers were more inclined to chase output growth aggressively during periods of firm commodity pricing, only to face strain when conditions reversed. The current generation of energy majors, including the company profiled here, has generally shifted toward a framework that prioritizes free cash generation, measured capital spending, and steady distribution to equity owners over rapid volume growth. That shift has been part of what has made energy value names more palatable to market participants who prioritize durability over rapid appreciation, and the maintained distribution in the latest update reinforces that this approach remains intact. Beyond company-specific results, the broader environment for crude and refined products continues to shape how energy value names are read by the market. Global crude conditions have remained comparatively steady in recent stretches, without the kind of dramatic supply disruption or demand collapse that has periodically rattled the sector in past cycles. Refining conditions, meanwhile, have held at levels that continue to support healthy throughput economics across much of the industry, providing a supportive backdrop for integrated operators with meaningful downstream exposure. This steadiness matters because energy value names tend to be judged less on whether commodity pricing is rising sharply and more on whether the operating environment is stable enough to support consistent execution. A market defined by wild commodity swings tends to make it harder for market participants to have confidence in near-term earnings trajectories, whereas a steadier backdrop allows companies with strong operational execution to demonstrate that execution more clearly. The current environment, characterized by measured global crude conditions and healthy refining economics, appears to be providing exactly that kind of setting for names like the one at the center of this update. One of the more notable structural themes shaping how the market views energy names this year has little to do with crude pricing directly and everything to do with electricity. The rapid build-out of artificial-intelligence infrastructure, particularly large data-center campuses designed to support intensive computing workloads, has driven a level of power demand that many grid operators and energy suppliers did not anticipate even a few years back. This has created a new and somewhat unexpected driver of interest in traditional energy names, since natural gas in particular has emerged as a favored fuel source for meeting incremental power needs tied to this build-out. For an integrated energy major with meaningful natural gas production and infrastructure, this dynamic represents a structural driver worth watching closely, even though it sits somewhat apart from the traditional narrative around crude pricing and refining margins. Market participants have increasingly begun weighing how exposed different energy names are to this power-demand theme, and companies with flexible natural gas supply positions are being examined with particular interest as a result. This is one of several threads knitting together what might otherwise look like separate stories, namely the steady performance of legacy energy majors and the rapid expansion of computing infrastructure tied to artificial intelligence. Refining and chemicals operations remain a critical piece of the puzzle for understanding how an integrated energy major generates earnings across a full cycle. Downstream margin dynamics are shaped by a combination of factors, including the spread between crude input costs and finished product pricing, the utilization rates achieved across a refining network, and the mix of products a given set of facilities is configured to produce. In recent periods, refining margins across much of the industry have held at levels that continue to support healthy downstream earnings, providing a meaningful complement to upstream production revenue. The company's downstream footprint spans a global network of facilities, giving it exposure to multiple regional refining markets rather than concentration in a single geography. This diversification tends to smooth out some of the volatility that can arise when a single region experiences a supply disruption, planned maintenance, or an unplanned outage. Combined with a chemicals business that produces feedstocks and intermediate products used across numerous industrial applications, the downstream side of the operation continues to function as a stabilizing counterweight to the more commodity-sensitive upstream business, reinforcing the integrated model's broader appeal to those examining energy value names. Within the competitive landscape of global energy majors, the company occupies a position defined by scale, balance-sheet strength, and a long track record of consistent capital distribution to equity owners. Compared with peers, it has generally been characterized by a conservative approach to leverage, favoring a capital structure that leaves room to maintain distributions and fund development programs even during periods of softer commodity pricing. This conservative stance has occasionally meant slower headline growth relative to peers willing to take on more leverage during favorable periods, but it has also tended to support steadier performance during downturns. Market participants examining the broader energy value stock landscape often compare integrated majors on the basis of breakeven economics, downstream diversification, and distribution consistency, three areas where the company profiled here has generally been viewed favorably. Its scale also affords it access to capital and project economics that smaller independent producers frequently cannot match, allowing it to pursue large, long-life developments that support output over extended periods. That contrast, chip-sector wobbles set against software-sector strength, has left parts of the market feeling unsettled even as headline indices sit near their highs. Looking beyond the immediate quarterly update, several structural themes continue to shape how energy majors, and the company in particular, are likely to be examined by the market in coming periods. The pace of the global energy transition remains a persistent thread, with companies across the sector continuing to balance traditional hydrocarbon production against measured capital deployment toward lower-carbon initiatives. How aggressively, or conservatively, a given company pursues that balance continues to factor into how market participants assess long-term positioning. Power demand tied to artificial-intelligence infrastructure represents another structural theme likely to remain relevant well beyond the current reporting season, given the scale of data-center build-out programs currently underway across the country. Natural gas supply flexibility, in particular, is likely to remain a differentiator among energy majors as this theme continues to unfold. Meanwhile, global crude supply dynamics, including production decisions made by major exporting nations, will continue to shape the pricing backdrop against which integrated majors are measured. Taken together, these threads indicate that the current period of relative steadiness in the sector, and the firmer sentiment that has followed the latest update, will likely continue to be tested by a combination of commodity pricing shifts, energy transition dynamics, and the ongoing build-out of power-intensive computing infrastructure. title: Chevron Stock Jumps 3.3% as Hormuz Doubts Lift Oil - TradingView
content: Chevron CVX, the integrated energy heavyweight pumping oil and running refineries around the world, delivered $12.1 billion of second-quarter earnings before its shares jumped roughly 3.3% Monday morning. But this move is about more than one strong quarter. Brent crude was back near $85 per barrel as hopes for a quick reopening of the Strait of Hormuz took another hit, with Iran putting conditions on restoring shipping traffic. That flipped the oil trade fast. Crude had tumbled more than 7% the previous week as investors bet on diplomacy. Now geopolitical risk is back on the screen, and Chevron suddenly has a much stronger oil-price tailwind behind already booming production. The numbers show just how much firepower Chevron has if crude stays elevated. Production reached roughly 4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, including a record 2.08 million barrels from the U.S. Upstream earnings hit $8.2 billion, while downstream profit climbed to $4.9 billion as stronger refining margins kicked in. U.S. refineries processed more than 1 million barrels per day, another record. That is the setup investors want from an integrated oil giant: more barrels, stronger refining economics and higher crude prices hitting at the same time. Add the Hess integration and $6.5 billion returned through dividends and buybacks during the quarter, and Chevron has a serious cash machine working underneath the geopolitical headlines. There is one catch: the stock is no bargain. GuruFocus puts Chevron at $192.63 versus a GF Value estimate of $158.06, meaning the shares trade about 21.87% above GF Value. That is a chunky premium, and it raises the bar from here. If oil stays high, record production keeps climbing and Hess delivers the expected boost, Chevron could grow into that valuation. If Hormuz tensions fade and crude rolls over, investors are suddenly holding an expensive oil stock into a weaker commodity tape. Chevron has the production, the cash flow and the oil-price momentum. What it does not have right now is much room for disappointment. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Select reference data provided by FactSet. Roughly 20 million barrels of petroleum liquids — about 20% of global consumption — passed through the waterway in 2024, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. That makes the strait more than a shipping lane. It gives Iran a relatively inexpensive way to threaten a huge portion of the world’s oil supply. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Washington wants to change that equation, calling the strait potentially “irrelevant” within two years as more oil moves through pipelines. For Chevron (NYSE:CVX | CVX Price Prediction), that’s more than a geopolitical talking point. The company is already involved in studying one of those potential escape routes: a pipeline connecting Iraq’s oil network to Syria’s Mediterranean coast. Iraq’s Haditha-Baniyas pipeline is important because it illustrates the broader idea: move oil overland to export terminals outside the Persian Gulf rather than forcing every barrel through Hormuz. The proposed route would connect Iraq’s oil network at Haditha with Syria’s Mediterranean port of Baniyas. It is closely related to the historic Kirkuk-Baniyas corridor, which once transported Iraqi crude through Syria to the Mediterranean. However, the current proposal is not simply a restoration of the old pipeline. More importantly, Iraq is only one piece of the puzzle. The EIA estimates Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have about 4.7 million barrels per day of unused pipeline capacity that can bypass Hormuz. That’s nowhere near the roughly 20 million barrels per day that crossed the strait in 2024, which explains why Washington cannot make Hormuz irrelevant with one pipeline project. It needs a network. That’s where Chevron gets interesting. The oil giant is participating in studies for the Haditha-Baniyas project alongside Iraq and Syria. If the project eventually moves from feasibility studies to construction, the company could gain a role in developing infrastructure connecting Middle Eastern oil to Mediterranean markets. But the bigger investment thesis is strategic. Every barrel that can reach a Mediterranean or Red Sea terminal without passing through Hormuz reduces the amount of traffic that has to be protected in the strait. That potentially reduces the military burden of keeping the waterway open — particularly important after a prolonged conflict has consumed precision missiles and air-defense interceptors. The U.S. military has reportedly depleted large portions of several missile inventories during the Iran war and after years of supporting Ukraine. Rebuilding those inventories will take money, production capacity, and time. That creates a second reason for Washington to favor infrastructure over perpetual military protection: a pipeline is a permanent piece of energy infrastructure, while interceptors are one-time expenditures.
